schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE PERSON (
    PERSONID INT,
    FIRSTNAME VARCHAR(255),
    LASTNAME VARCHAR(255),
    PRIMARY KEY (PERSONID)
);

CREATE TABLE ADDRESS (
    ADDRESSID INT,
    PERSONID INT,
    CITY VARCHAR(255),
    STATE VARCHAR(255),
    PRIMARY KEY (ADDRESSID, PERSONID),
    FOREIGN KEY (PERSONID) REFERENCES PERSON(PERSONID)
);
q1: SELECT FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE FROM PERSON AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN ADDRESS AS A ON P.PERSONID = A.PERSONID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE FROM PERSON AS P LEFT JOIN ADDRESS AS A ON P.PERSONID = A.PERSONID
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE FROM PERSON AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN ADDRESS AS A ON P.PERSONID = A.PERSONID
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT FIRSTNAME, LASTNAME, CITY, STATE FROM PERSON AS P LEFT JOIN ADDRESS AS A ON P.PERSONID = A.PERSONID
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 can return duplicate rows when a person has multiple addresses, while Q2 uses DISTINCT to ensure unique rows. The difference arises from the presence of the DISTINCT keyword in Q2, which Q1 lacks.
counterexample_dsp: A person with multiple addresses in the ADDRESS table will produce duplicate rows in Q1 but only one row in Q2. This triggers the difference.
